## Career
### Early career
Maher began his career as a comedian and actor. He was host of the New York City comedy club Catch a Rising Star in 1979. Maher began appearing on Johnny Carson's and David Letterman's shows in 1982.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-21) In 1984 he served as "announcer and sidekick"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-22) in all six episodes of the Disney Channel's _Steve Allen's Music Room_.
He made limited television appearances including on _Sara_ (1985),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-NYT-23)_Max Headroom_ (1987),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-24)_Murder, She Wrote_ (1989, 1990),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-NYT-23) and _Charlie Hoover_ (1991). His feature film debut was in _D.C. Cab_ (1983).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-NYT-23) He later appeared in _Ratboy_ (1986),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-NYT-23)_House II: The Second Story_ (1987),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-NYT-23)_Cannibal Women in the Avocado Jungle of Death_ (1988),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-NYT-23)_Newhart_ (1988), hosted the talk show _Midnight Hour_ on CBS (1990) and appeared in _Pizza Man_ (1991).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-NYT-23)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Politically Incorrect with Bill Maher_
Seth MacFarlane speaking at a ceremony for Maher to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in September 2010
Maher assumed the host role on _Politically Incorrect with Bill Maher_, a late-night political talk show that ran on Comedy Central from 1993 to 1997 and on ABC from 1997 to 2002. The show regularly began with a topical monologue by Maher preceding the introduction of four guests, usually a diverse group of individuals, such as show business, popular culture, political pundits, political consultants, authors, and occasionally news figures. The group would discuss topical issues selected by Maher, who also participated in the discussions.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-nytimes-25)Jerry Seinfeld, a regular guest on the show, stated that _Politically Incorrect_ reminded him of talk shows from the 1950s and '60s "when guests interacted with each other as much as with the host".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-nytimes-25)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Politically Incorrect with Bill Maher_
_Politically Incorrect_ won an array of awards, including an Emmy Award for Outstanding Technical Direction, two CableACE awards for Best Talk Show Series, and a Genesis Award for Best Television Talk Show. Maher earned numerous award nominations for his producing, writing, and hosting of _Politically Incorrect_, including ten Emmy nominations, two TV Guide nominations, and two Writers Guild nominations. ABC decided against renewing Maher's contract for _Politically Incorrect_ in 2002, after he made a controversial on-air remark six days after the September 11 attacks.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-26) He agreed with his guest, conservative pundit [Dinesh D'Souza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinesh_D'Souza "Dinesh D'Souza"), that the 9/11 terrorists did not act in a cowardly manner (in rebuttal to President Bush's statement calling them cowards). Maher said, "We have been the cowards. Lobbing cruise missiles from 2,000 miles away. That's cowardly. Staying in the airplane when it hits the building. Say what you want about it. Not cowardly. You're right." Maher later clarified that his comment was not anti-military, referencing his well-documented and longstanding support for the American armed services.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-28) After receiving complaints, FedEx and Sears pulled their advertisements from the show, costing the show significant revenue.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Sayre-30)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Politically Incorrect with Bill Maher_
Maher's remarks after 9/11 were not the first time he had sparked controversy on _Politically Incorrect_. In the same year, he expressed his deep regrets and apologized after being widely criticized for comparing his dogs to mentally disabled children.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-31) The show was canceled on June 16, 2002; the Sinclair Broadcast Group had dropped the show from its ABC-affiliated stations several months earlier. On June 22, 2002, six days after the cancellation of _Politically Incorrect_, Maher received the Los Angeles Press Club president's award (for "championing free speech").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Sayre-30) Maher was on the board of judges for the 2002 [PEN/Newman's Own First Amendment Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEN/Newman's_Own_First_Amendment_Award "PEN/Newman's Own First Amendment Award"), which was given to writer Vanessa Leggett, imprisoned for 168 days for protecting sources and research notes.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-32)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
In 2003, Maher became the host, co-producer, and co-writer of _Real Time with Bill Maher_, a weekly hour-long political comedy talk show on the cable television network HBO. In 2016, HBO renewed _Real Time_ through 2018, for its 15th and 16th seasons.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-33) During an interview, Maher told Terry Gross (on NPR's _Fresh Air_) that he much prefers having serious and well-informed guests on his program, as opposed to the random celebrities that fleshed out his roundtable discussions on _Politically Incorrect_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-34) After appearing on HBO on Fridays, _Real Time_ is re-broadcast on CNN on Saturdays.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-36)
As with his previous show, _Politically Incorrect_, Maher begins _Real Time_ with a comic opening monologue based upon current events and other topical issues. He proceeds to a one-on-one interview with a guest, either in-studio or via satellite. Following the interview, Maher sits with two or three panelists—usually consisting of pundits, authors, activists, actors, politicians, and journalists—for a discussion of the week's events.

## Career
### Television career
#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
_Real Time_ has earned widespread praise. It has been nominated for more than ten Primetime Emmy Awards and six Writer's Guild awards. In 2007, Maher and his co-producers were awarded the Television Producer of the Year Award in Variety Television by the Producers Guild of America.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-37) Maher holds the record for the most Emmy nominations without a win, having been nominated on 22 occasions and not winning once. Eleven of the nominations were for _Politically Incorrect_, while nine were for _Real Time_. The other two were nominations for two of his HBO comedy specials: _[I'm Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm\_Swiss "I'm Swiss")_ and _Bill Maher: The Decider_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-38)
Maher is a frequent commentator on various cable news networks, including CNN, MSNBC, Fox News, and HLN. Maher has regularly appeared on CNN's _The Situation Room with Wolf Blitzer_[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-39) and has also been a frequent guest on MSNBC's _Hardball with Chris Matthews_,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-40)_The Rachel Maddow Show_,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-41) and _Countdown with Keith Olbermann_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-42) Maher has also appeared as a guest on HLN's _The Joy Behar Show_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-43) He wrote the foreword for the 2002 book, _Spin This!: All the Ways We Don't Tell the Truth_ by show host Bill Press.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-44)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
Maher hosted the January 13, 2006, edition of _Larry King Live_, on which he was a frequent guest. Maher appeared as a special guest on the June 29, 2010, edition of the show, on which CNN anchor Larry King announced his retirement.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-45) Maher co-emceed the final show of _Larry King Live_ on December 16, 2010, with Ryan Seacrest.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-46)

## Career
### Other work
In 2004, Maher appeared on stage as Satan in The Steve Allen Theater production of "Hollywood Hell House", a spoof of Christian-run hell houses. The show was a faithful reproduction of an evangelistic scare-experience written by Reverend Keenan Roberts to terrify teenagers into declaring themselves Christians. "Our faith is that putting this up as itself, it will hoist itself on its own petard, that it's comical just as it is," explained producer Maggie Rowe. The show featured a rotating cast of over 160 celebrities, including Andy Richter (Jesus), Richard Belzer, Dave Thomas, Traci Lords, Craig Bierko, Sarah Silverman, and Julia Sweeney.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-47) Maher and director Larry Charles teamed up to make the movie _Religulous_, described by trade publication _Variety_ as a documentary "that spoofs religious extremism across the world". It was released on October 3, 2008.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-49)
In 2013, Maher became one of the executive producers for the HBO newsmagazine series _Vice_.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-51) Also in 2013, Maher appeared on _The Tonight Show with Jay Leno_ and offered to pay $5 million to a charity if Donald Trump would produce his birth certificate, a challenge meant to disprove a joke that Trump was the son of an orangutan. Maher said this in response to Trump having previously challenged President Barack Obama to produce his birth certificate, and having offered $5 million payable to a charity of Obama's choice if Obama would produce his college applications, transcripts, and passport records.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Allen6Feb-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Lee1Nov-53)

## Career
### Other work
In response to Maher's offer, Trump produced his birth certificate, and then Trump launched a lawsuit after Maher was not forthcoming, claiming that Maher's $5 million offer was legally binding. "I don't think he was joking", Trump said. "He said it with venom."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Allen6Feb-52) Trump withdrew his lawsuit against the comedian after eight weeks.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Ax3April-54)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
Maher considers himself to be at odds with both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-News_1-74) In the 2008 U.S. presidential election, Maher announced his support for U.S. Senator Barack Obama (D-IL).[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-75) Although Maher welcomed Obama's electoral victory, he soon became critical of the new president for not acting more boldly on health care reform and other liberal issues.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-76) On February 23, 2012, after his "Crazy Stupid Politics" special streamed on Yahoo! Screen, Maher announced that he was contributing $1 million to Priorities USA, the Obama SuperPAC.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-78) Maher has voted for Bob Dole and Ralph Nader.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-News_1-74)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
In the lead-up to the 2014 midterm elections, Maher conducted a "Flip a District" contest on his HBO show. His audience was asked to select one "terrible, entrenched" member of Congress in a close election race—"the loserest loser of all"—to remove from office. Maher aimed to help oust that representative by shining a "national spotlight" on the politician during segments of his show and stand-up comedy appearances in that member's district during the Fall election.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-80) Maher ultimately selected Republican Representative John Kline from Minnesota's [2nd congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota's_2nd_congressional_district "Minnesota's 2nd congressional district"), but he failed to prevent him from winning against his Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party opponent Mike Obermueller.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-81)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
In the 2016 U.S. presidential election, Maher initially endorsed Senator Bernie Sanders on February 5, 2016. Maher later announced his support for Hillary Clinton after Clinton won the nomination from the Democratic Party primary elections in June 2016.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-82) In October 2016, Maher criticized WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange for publishing leaks from the DNC's emails, saying: "I really feel like he's lost his way a little, and he hates Hillary."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-83) On March 31, 2017, following her defeat, Maher responded on air to suggestions Clinton was ready to end her low profile and speak out: "Hillary, stay in the woods. Okay. You had your shot. You fucked it up. You're Bill Buckner. We had the World Series, and you let the grounder go through your legs. Let someone else have the chance."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-84) In August 2019, Maher said an economic recession would be "worth it" if Donald Trump did not get re-elected in 2020. He said: "We have survived many recessions. We can't survive another Donald Trump term."[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-85)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
Over the course of 20 different editions of _Real Time with Bill Maher_ broadcast between April 13, 2018, and August 7, 2020,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-86) and in several press interviews,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-87) Maher predicted that Trump would refuse to concede any loss in the 2020 United States presidential election, dedicating a 'New Rules' end segment to the subject on January 25, 2020.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-88) Maher highlighted Trump's own public references to Maher's assertions that Trump was "not going to leave", and quoted Trump's March 14, 2019, assertion, "I have the support of the police, the military, the bikers [for Trump]" and "the tough people",[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-89) citing this as evidence that Trump would seek to remain in office by force. Maher predicted there would be violence by armed Trump supporters attempting to keep Trump in power and criticized Democratic Party politicians for not taking the threat seriously:

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
> "So my question to all Democratic candidates is: what's the plan? If you win, and the next day he claims he's voiding the election because of irregularities he's hearing about, what do you do? What do you do when the crowd that was in Virginia this week, 22,000 strong, marches on Washington? This is a scary moment. And when I've asked Democrats, 'What do we do if he doesn't go?', their answer is always some variation of 'We have to win big!'... First of all, NO! No, we don't have to win by a landslide! Jesus, fucking Democrats! I am so sick of Democrats volunteering to play by two different sets of rules. That's the new paradigm? Republicans can win by one vote, but we're not legitimate unless it's a landslide? Fuck. And two, do you really think it would matter if it was? That they would suddenly get rational about math and facts? They believe Hillary ran a pedophile ring out of a pizza parlor!"
Maher later said in an August 15, 2020, interview with _Vanity Fair_ that "we've baked it into the cake that he's not going to leave."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-90) In the September 25, 2020, edition of _Real Time_, Maher criticized the framing of a _New York Times_ story by Michael Crowley headlined "Trump Won't Commit to Peaceful Transfer of Power", which ran on page 15 of the print edition of the paper. Maher asserted, "I got no help from the _New York Times_, _Washington Post_, [or] CNN", adding that the media "should have amplified" the severity of Trump's threats that he would refuse to concede or commit to a peaceful transition of power.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-91)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Politically Incorrect with Bill Maher_
_Politically Incorrect_ won an array of awards, including an Emmy Award for Outstanding Technical Direction, two CableACE awards for Best Talk Show Series, and a Genesis Award for Best Television Talk Show. Maher earned numerous award nominations for his producing, writing, and hosting of _Politically Incorrect_, including ten Emmy nominations, two TV Guide nominations, and two Writers Guild nominations. ABC decided against renewing Maher's contract for _Politically Incorrect_ in 2002, after he made a controversial on-air remark six days after the September 11 attacks.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-26) He agreed with his guest, conservative pundit [Dinesh D'Souza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinesh_D'Souza "Dinesh D'Souza"), that the 9/11 terrorists did not act in a cowardly manner (in rebuttal to President Bush's statement calling them cowards). Maher said, "We have been the cowards. Lobbing cruise missiles from 2,000 miles away. That's cowardly. Staying in the airplane when it hits the building. Say what you want about it. Not cowardly. You're right." Maher later clarified that his comment was not anti-military, referencing his well-documented and longstanding support for the American armed services.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-28) After receiving complaints, FedEx and Sears pulled their advertisements from the show, costing the show significant revenue.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Sayre-30)

## Career

#### _Politically Incorrect with Bill Maher_
Maher's remarks after 9/11 were not the first time he had sparked controversy on _Politically Incorrect_. In the same year, he expressed his deep regrets and apologized after being widely criticized for comparing his dogs to mentally disabled children.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-31) The show was canceled on June 16, 2002; the Sinclair Broadcast Group had dropped the show from its ABC-affiliated stations several months earlier. On June 22, 2002, six days after the cancellation of _Politically Incorrect_, Maher received the Los Angeles Press Club president's award (for "championing free speech").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Sayre-30) Maher was on the board of judges for the 2002 [PEN/Newman's Own First Amendment Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEN/Newman's_Own_First_Amendment_Award "PEN/Newman's Own First Amendment Award"), which was given to writer Vanessa Leggett, imprisoned for 168 days for protecting sources and research notes.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-32)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
In 2003, Maher became the host, co-producer, and co-writer of _Real Time with Bill Maher_, a weekly hour-long political comedy talk show on the cable television network HBO. In 2016, HBO renewed _Real Time_ through 2018, for its 15th and 16th seasons.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-33) During an interview, Maher told Terry Gross (on NPR's _Fresh Air_) that he much prefers having serious and well-informed guests on his program, as opposed to the random celebrities that fleshed out his roundtable discussions on _Politically Incorrect_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-34) After appearing on HBO on Fridays, _Real Time_ is re-broadcast on CNN on Saturdays.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-36)
As with his previous show, _Politically Incorrect_, Maher begins _Real Time_ with a comic opening monologue based upon current events and other topical issues. He proceeds to a one-on-one interview with a guest, either in-studio or via satellite. Following the interview, Maher sits with two or three panelists—usually consisting of pundits, authors, activists, actors, politicians, and journalists—for a discussion of the week's events.

## Career

#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
_Real Time_ has earned widespread praise. It has been nominated for more than ten Primetime Emmy Awards and six Writer's Guild awards. In 2007, Maher and his co-producers were awarded the Television Producer of the Year Award in Variety Television by the Producers Guild of America.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-37) Maher holds the record for the most Emmy nominations without a win, having been nominated on 22 occasions and not winning once. Eleven of the nominations were for _Politically Incorrect_, while nine were for _Real Time_. The other two were nominations for two of his HBO comedy specials: _[I'm Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm\_Swiss "I'm Swiss")_ and _Bill Maher: The Decider_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-38)
Maher is a frequent commentator on various cable news networks, including CNN, MSNBC, Fox News, and HLN. Maher has regularly appeared on CNN's _The Situation Room with Wolf Blitzer_[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-39) and has also been a frequent guest on MSNBC's _Hardball with Chris Matthews_,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-40)_The Rachel Maddow Show_,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-41) and _Countdown with Keith Olbermann_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-42) Maher has also appeared as a guest on HLN's _The Joy Behar Show_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-43) He wrote the foreword for the 2002 book, _Spin This!: All the Ways We Don't Tell the Truth_ by show host Bill Press.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-44)

In 2004, Maher appeared on stage as Satan in The Steve Allen Theater production of "Hollywood Hell House", a spoof of Christian-run hell houses. In the lead-up to the 2014 midterm elections, Maher conducted a "Flip a District" contest on his HBO show. His audience was asked to select one "terrible, entrenched" member of Congress in a close election race—"the loserest loser of all"—to remove from office. Maher aimed to help oust that representative by shining a "national spotlight" on the politician during segments of his show and stand-up comedy appearances in that member's district during the Fall election.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-80) Maher ultimately selected Republican Representative John Kline from Minnesota's [2nd congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota's_2nd_congressional_district "Minnesota's 2nd congressional district"), but he failed to prevent him from winning against his Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party opponent Mike Obermueller.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-81)

Maher said, "We have been the cowards. Lobbing cruise missiles from 2,000 miles away. That's cowardly. Staying in the airplane when it hits the building. Say what you want about it. Not cowardly. You're right." Maher later clarified that his comment was not anti-military, referencing his well-documented and longstanding support for the American armed services.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-28) After receiving complaints, FedEx and Sears pulled their advertisements from the show, costing the show significant revenue.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Sayre-30)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Politically Incorrect with Bill Maher_
Maher's remarks after 9/11 were not the first time he had sparked controversy on _Politically Incorrect_. In the same year, he expressed his deep regrets and apologized after being widely criticized for comparing his dogs to mentally disabled children.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-31) The show was canceled on June 16, 2002; the Sinclair Broadcast Group had dropped the show from its ABC-affiliated stations several months earlier. On June 22, 2002, six days after the cancellation of _Politically Incorrect_, Maher received the Los Angeles Press Club president's award (for "championing free speech").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Sayre-30) Maher was on the board of judges for the 2002 [PEN/Newman's Own First Amendment Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEN/Newman's_Own_First_Amendment_Award "PEN/Newman's Own First Amendment Award"), which was given to writer Vanessa Leggett, imprisoned for 168 days for protecting sources and research notes.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-32)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
In 2003, Maher became the host, co-producer, and co-writer of _Real Time with Bill Maher_, a weekly hour-long political comedy talk show on the cable television network HBO. In 2016, HBO renewed _Real Time_ through 2018, for its 15th and 16th seasons.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-33) During an interview, Maher told Terry Gross (on NPR's _Fresh Air_) that he much prefers having serious and well-informed guests on his program, as opposed to the random celebrities that fleshed out his roundtable discussions on _Politically Incorrect_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-34) After appearing on HBO on Fridays, _Real Time_ is re-broadcast on CNN on Saturdays.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-36)
As with his previous show, _Politically Incorrect_, Maher begins _Real Time_ with a comic opening monologue based upon current events and other topical issues. He proceeds to a one-on-one interview with a guest, either in-studio or via satellite. Following the interview, Maher sits with two or three panelists—usually consisting of pundits, authors, activists, actors, politicians, and journalists—for a discussion of the week's events.

## Career
### Television career
#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
_Real Time_ has earned widespread praise. It has been nominated for more than ten Primetime Emmy Awards and six Writer's Guild awards. In 2007, Maher and his co-producers were awarded the Television Producer of the Year Award in Variety Television by the Producers Guild of America.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-37) Maher holds the record for the most Emmy nominations without a win, having been nominated on 22 occasions and not winning once. Eleven of the nominations were for _Politically Incorrect_, while nine were for _Real Time_. The other two were nominations for two of his HBO comedy specials: _[I'm Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm\_Swiss "I'm Swiss")_ and _Bill Maher: The Decider_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-38)
Maher is a frequent commentator on various cable news networks, including CNN, MSNBC, Fox News, and HLN. Maher has regularly appeared on CNN's _The Situation Room with Wolf Blitzer_[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-39) and has also been a frequent guest on MSNBC's _Hardball with Chris Matthews_,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-40)_The Rachel Maddow Show_,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-41) and _Countdown with Keith Olbermann_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-42) Maher has also appeared as a guest on HLN's _The Joy Behar Show_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-43) He wrote the foreword for the 2002 book, _Spin This!: All the Ways We Don't Tell the Truth_ by show host Bill Press.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-44)

## Career
### Television career
#### _Real Time with Bill Maher_
Maher hosted the January 13, 2006, edition of _Larry King Live_, on which he was a frequent guest. Maher appeared as a special guest on the June 29, 2010, edition of the show, on which CNN anchor Larry King announced his retirement.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-45) Maher co-emceed the final show of _Larry King Live_ on December 16, 2010, with Ryan Seacrest.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-46)

## Career
### Other work
In 2004, Maher appeared on stage as Satan in The Steve Allen Theater production of "Hollywood Hell House", a spoof of Christian-run hell houses. The show was a faithful reproduction of an evangelistic scare-experience written by Reverend Keenan Roberts to terrify teenagers into declaring themselves Christians. "Our faith is that putting this up as itself, it will hoist itself on its own petard, that it's comical just as it is," explained producer Maggie Rowe. The show featured a rotating cast of over 160 celebrities, including Andy Richter (Jesus), Richard Belzer, Dave Thomas, Traci Lords, Craig Bierko, Sarah Silverman, and Julia Sweeney.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-47) Maher and director Larry Charles teamed up to make the movie _Religulous_, described by trade publication _Variety_ as a documentary "that spoofs religious extremism across the world". It was released on October 3, 2008.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-49)
In 2013, Maher became one of the executive producers for the HBO newsmagazine series _Vice_.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-51) Also in 2013, Maher appeared on _The Tonight Show with Jay Leno_ and offered to pay $5 million to a charity if Donald Trump would produce his birth certificate, a challenge meant to disprove a joke that Trump was the son of an orangutan. Maher said this in response to Trump having previously challenged President Barack Obama to produce his birth certificate, and having offered $5 million payable to a charity of Obama's choice if Obama would produce his college applications, transcripts, and passport records.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Allen6Feb-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Lee1Nov-53)

## Career
### Other work
In response to Maher's offer, Trump produced his birth certificate, and then Trump launched a lawsuit after Maher was not forthcoming, claiming that Maher's $5 million offer was legally binding. "I don't think he was joking", Trump said. "He said it with venom."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Allen6Feb-52) Trump withdrew his lawsuit against the comedian after eight weeks.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-Ax3April-54)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
Maher considers himself to be at odds with both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-News_1-74) In the 2008 U.S. presidential election, Maher announced his support for U.S. Senator Barack Obama (D-IL).[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-75) Although Maher welcomed Obama's electoral victory, he soon became critical of the new president for not acting more boldly on health care reform and other liberal issues.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-76) On February 23, 2012, after his "Crazy Stupid Politics" special streamed on Yahoo! Screen, Maher announced that he was contributing $1 million to Priorities USA, the Obama SuperPAC.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-78) Maher has voted for Bob Dole and Ralph Nader.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-News_1-74)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
In the lead-up to the 2014 midterm elections, Maher conducted a "Flip a District" contest on his HBO show. His audience was asked to select one "terrible, entrenched" member of Congress in a close election race—"the loserest loser of all"—to remove from office. Maher aimed to help oust that representative by shining a "national spotlight" on the politician during segments of his show and stand-up comedy appearances in that member's district during the Fall election.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-80) Maher ultimately selected Republican Representative John Kline from Minnesota's [2nd congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota's_2nd_congressional_district "Minnesota's 2nd congressional district"), but he failed to prevent him from winning against his Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party opponent Mike Obermueller.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-81)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
In the 2016 U.S. presidential election, Maher initially endorsed Senator Bernie Sanders on February 5, 2016. Maher later announced his support for Hillary Clinton after Clinton won the nomination from the Democratic Party primary elections in June 2016.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-82) In October 2016, Maher criticized WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange for publishing leaks from the DNC's emails, saying: "I really feel like he's lost his way a little, and he hates Hillary."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-83) On March 31, 2017, following her defeat, Maher responded on air to suggestions Clinton was ready to end her low profile and speak out: "Hillary, stay in the woods. Okay. You had your shot. You fucked it up. You're Bill Buckner. We had the World Series, and you let the grounder go through your legs. Let someone else have the chance."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-84) In August 2019, Maher said an economic recession would be "worth it" if Donald Trump did not get re-elected in 2020. He said: "We have survived many recessions. We can't survive another Donald Trump term."[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-85)

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
Over the course of 20 different editions of _Real Time with Bill Maher_ broadcast between April 13, 2018, and August 7, 2020,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-86) and in several press interviews,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-87) Maher predicted that Trump would refuse to concede any loss in the 2020 United States presidential election, dedicating a 'New Rules' end segment to the subject on January 25, 2020.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-88) Maher highlighted Trump's own public references to Maher's assertions that Trump was "not going to leave", and quoted Trump's March 14, 2019, assertion, "I have the support of the police, the military, the bikers [for Trump]" and "the tough people",[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-89) citing this as evidence that Trump would seek to remain in office by force. Maher predicted there would be violence by armed Trump supporters attempting to keep Trump in power and criticized Democratic Party politicians for not taking the threat seriously:

## Political views
### Candidates and endorsements
> "So my question to all Democratic candidates is: what's the plan? If you win, and the next day he claims he's voiding the election because of irregularities he's hearing about, what do you do? What do you do when the crowd that was in Virginia this week, 22,000 strong, marches on Washington? This is a scary moment. And when I've asked Democrats, 'What do we do if he doesn't go?', their answer is always some variation of 'We have to win big!'... First of all, NO! No, we don't have to win by a landslide! Jesus, fucking Democrats! I am so sick of Democrats volunteering to play by two different sets of rules. That's the new paradigm? Republicans can win by one vote, but we're not legitimate unless it's a landslide? Fuck. And two, do you really think it would matter if it was? That they would suddenly get rational about math and facts? They believe Hillary ran a pedophile ring out of a pizza parlor!"
Maher later said in an August 15, 2020, interview with _Vanity Fair_ that "we've baked it into the cake that he's not going to leave."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-90) In the September 25, 2020, edition of _Real Time_, Maher criticized the framing of a _New York Times_ story by Michael Crowley headlined "Trump Won't Commit to Peaceful Transfer of Power", which ran on page 15 of the print edition of the paper. Maher asserted, "I got no help from the _New York Times_, _Washington Post_, [or] CNN", adding that the media "should have amplified" the severity of Trump's threats that he would refuse to concede or commit to a peaceful transition of power.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher#cite_note-91)

_**Real Time with Bill Maher**_ is an American television talk show created, written and presented by Bill Maher, and has been airing on HBO since 2003, with an audio-only podcast, with episodes at least since 2015.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-megaphone/WMHY1886903044-1) Much like his previous series _Politically Incorrect_ on Comedy Central and later on ABC, _Real Time_ features a panel of guests who discuss current events in politics and the media. Unlike the previous show, guests are usually better versed in the subject matter; more experts such as journalists, professors, and politicians participate in the panel, and fewer actors and celebrities are included.

_Real Time_ is a weekly hour-long program with a studio audience, and is broadcast from Studio 33 (_The Price Is Right_ studio) at Television City in Los Angeles. Prior to Season 20, the program aired live on Friday nights at 10:00 pm ET, however, it is now pre-recorded at 7:00 pm ET. In addition, a 10–15-minute "Overtime" segment quickly follows the show on YouTube live stream, which answers questions posted by viewers through HBO's online website for the show. The Overtime segment was added to CNN Tonight programming in 2023.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-2)
The twenty-fourth season premiered on January 23, 2026.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-3) In January 2026, HBO announced that the series had been renewed for two additional seasons, keeping the show on the air through its twenty-sixth season, which will run through the end of 2028.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-4) After appearing on HBO on Fridays, _Real Time_ is re-broadcast on CNN on Saturdays.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-6)
The opening sequence contains a theme song composed by Scott "Shavoni" Parker, Christopher "Kid" Reid and Louis Brown. A montage of animated graphics with political and cultural themes surrounded by splashes of color accompanies the music.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-7) Season 21 features an updated version of the theme song performed by Green Day.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-8)

The show opens with a comedy monologue performed by Maher, followed by a one-on-one interview with a prominent guest. Maher then engages with two or three additional panel guests, who partake in various discussions and debates. Midway through the panel session, Maher performs a comedic bit that typically satirizes a notable current event. The final segment of each episode is entitled "New Rules" and contains an array of editorials related to popular culture and American politics.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-9) The final "New Rule" serves as Maher's closing editorial monologue. While the aforementioned format is typically followed, Maher states that it is not entirely rigid and has also indicated that he prefers in-studio interviews to satellite interviews.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-Wrap-10)
Since the show airs on HBO, Maher and his guests are allowed to use profane language, a significant departure from the broadcast standards that existed on _Politically Incorrect_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-11) Graphics displayed throughout the show may also contain some uncensored content.
During the first season, Paul F. Tompkins was featured as a correspondent, and each episode would conclude with a performance by a stand-up comedian. The segments featuring Tompkins and the stand-up comedians were dropped after episode 10. Viewers were also able to engage over the air during the first season by calling in live, but this practice was subsequently discontinued._[citation needed_]
Starting with episode 67, audio-only versions of the show were made available as free podcasts via the iTunes Store[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-12) and as raw RSS feeds.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-13) The podcasts may also feature bonus material taped during studio rehearsal, such as additional "New Rules" that were not included in the final broadcast.

During Season 4, Maher began hosting a live chat (now called "Overtime") with his guests immediately following each broadcast. Viewers are invited to submit questions and topics for Maher and the other participants to answer and discuss. This post-show event was initially featured on HBO's website[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-14) and is currently broadcast on CNN.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-15)

### Politics and current events
[edit]
Bill Maher in 2007
Maher has been a critic of the Obama administration,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-Wrap-10) the Bush administration and the Trump administration. His panel attempts to present a diverse set of views. Frequently, it consists of a liberal commentator or political figure, a conservative commentator or political figure, and a third individual who does not have as clear an ideological label, or someone with moderate beliefs. This third individual is often an actor, comedian, musician, or other entertainment figure, though many times the commentator is openly conservative or liberal.

_**Real Time with Bill Maher**_ is an American television talk show created, written and presented by Bill Maher, and has been airing on HBO since 2003, with an audio-only podcast, with episodes at least since 2015.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-megaphone/WMHY1886903044-1) Much like his previous series _Politically Incorrect_ on Comedy Central and later on ABC, _Real Time_ features a panel of guests who discuss current events in politics and the media. Unlike the previous show, guests are usually better versed in the subject matter; more experts such as journalists, professors, and politicians participate in the panel, and fewer actors and celebrities are included.
texts.1:
_Real Time_ is a weekly hour-long program with a studio audience, and is broadcast from Studio 33 (_The Price Is Right_ studio) at Television City in Los Angeles. Prior to Season 20, the program aired live on Friday nights at 10:00 pm ET, however, it is now pre-recorded at 7:00 pm ET. In addition, a 10–15-minute "Overtime" segment quickly follows the show on YouTube live stream, which answers questions posted by viewers through HBO's online website for the show. The Overtime segment was added to CNN Tonight programming in 2023.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-2)
The twenty-fourth season premiered on January 23, 2026.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-3) In January 2026, HBO announced that the series had been renewed for two additional seasons, keeping the show on the air through its twenty-sixth season, which will run through the end of 2028.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-4) After appearing on HBO on Fridays, _Real Time_ is re-broadcast on CNN on Saturdays.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-6)
The opening sequence contains a theme song composed by Scott "Shavoni" Parker, Christopher "Kid" Reid and Louis Brown. A montage of animated graphics with political and cultural themes surrounded by splashes of color accompanies the music.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-7) Season 21 features an updated version of the theme song performed by Green Day.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-8)
texts.2:
The show opens with a comedy monologue performed by Maher, followed by a one-on-one interview with a prominent guest. Maher then engages with two or three additional panel guests, who partake in various discussions and debates. Midway through the panel session, Maher performs a comedic bit that typically satirizes a notable current event. The final segment of each episode is entitled "New Rules" and contains an array of editorials related to popular culture and American politics.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-9) The final "New Rule" serves as Maher's closing editorial monologue. While the aforementioned format is typically followed, Maher states that it is not entirely rigid and has also indicated that he prefers in-studio interviews to satellite interviews.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-Wrap-10)
Since the show airs on HBO, Maher and his guests are allowed to use profane language, a significant departure from the broadcast standards that existed on _Politically Incorrect_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-11) Graphics displayed throughout the show may also contain some uncensored content.
During the first season, Paul F. Tompkins was featured as a correspondent, and each episode would conclude with a performance by a stand-up comedian. The segments featuring Tompkins and the stand-up comedians were dropped after episode 10. Viewers were also able to engage over the air during the first season by calling in live, but this practice was subsequently discontinued._[citation needed_]
Starting with episode 67, audio-only versions of the show were made available as free podcasts via the iTunes Store[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-12) and as raw RSS feeds.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-13) The podcasts may also feature bonus material taped during studio rehearsal, such as additional "New Rules" that were not included in the final broadcast.
texts.3: During Season 4, Maher began hosting a live chat (now called "Overtime") with his guests immediately following each broadcast. Viewers are invited to submit questions and topics for Maher and the other participants to answer and discuss. This post-show event was initially featured on HBO's website[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-14) and is currently broadcast on CNN.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-15)
texts.4:
### Politics and current events
[edit]
Bill Maher in 2007
Maher has been a critic of the Obama administration,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-Wrap-10) the Bush administration and the Trump administration. His panel attempts to present a diverse set of views. Frequently, it consists of a liberal commentator or political figure, a conservative commentator or political figure, and a third individual who does not have as clear an ideological label, or someone with moderate beliefs. This third individual is often an actor, comedian, musician, or other entertainment figure, though many times the commentator is openly conservative or liberal.

_**Real Time with Bill Maher**_ is an American television talk show created, written and presented by Bill Maher, and has been airing on HBO since 2003, with an audio-only podcast, with episodes at least since 2015.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-megaphone/WMHY1886903044-1) Much like his previous series _Politically Incorrect_ on Comedy Central and later on ABC, _Real Time_ features a panel of guests who discuss current events in politics and the media. Unlike the previous show, guests are usually better versed in the subject matter; more experts such as journalists, professors, and politicians participate in the panel, and fewer actors and celebrities are included.

_Real Time_ is a weekly hour-long program with a studio audience, and is broadcast from Studio 33 (_The Price Is Right_ studio) at Television City in Los Angeles. Prior to Season 20, the program aired live on Friday nights at 10:00 pm ET, however, it is now pre-recorded at 7:00 pm ET. In addition, a 10–15-minute "Overtime" segment quickly follows the show on YouTube live stream, which answers questions posted by viewers through HBO's online website for the show. The Overtime segment was added to CNN Tonight programming in 2023.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-2)
The twenty-fourth season premiered on January 23, 2026.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-3) In January 2026, HBO announced that the series had been renewed for two additional seasons, keeping the show on the air through its twenty-sixth season, which will run through the end of 2028.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-4) After appearing on HBO on Fridays, _Real Time_ is re-broadcast on CNN on Saturdays.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-6)
The opening sequence contains a theme song composed by Scott "Shavoni" Parker, Christopher "Kid" Reid and Louis Brown. A montage of animated graphics with political and cultural themes surrounded by splashes of color accompanies the music.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-7) Season 21 features an updated version of the theme song performed by Green Day.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-8)

The show opens with a comedy monologue performed by Maher, followed by a one-on-one interview with a prominent guest. Maher then engages with two or three additional panel guests, who partake in various discussions and debates. Midway through the panel session, Maher performs a comedic bit that typically satirizes a notable current event. The final segment of each episode is entitled "New Rules" and contains an array of editorials related to popular culture and American politics.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-9) The final "New Rule" serves as Maher's closing editorial monologue. While the aforementioned format is typically followed, Maher states that it is not entirely rigid and has also indicated that he prefers in-studio interviews to satellite interviews.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-Wrap-10)
Since the show airs on HBO, Maher and his guests are allowed to use profane language, a significant departure from the broadcast standards that existed on _Politically Incorrect_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-11) Graphics displayed throughout the show may also contain some uncensored content.
During the first season, Paul F. Tompkins was featured as a correspondent, and each episode would conclude with a performance by a stand-up comedian. The segments featuring Tompkins and the stand-up comedians were dropped after episode 10. Viewers were also able to engage over the air during the first season by calling in live, but this practice was subsequently discontinued._[citation needed_]
Starting with episode 67, audio-only versions of the show were made available as free podcasts via the iTunes Store[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-12) and as raw RSS feeds.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-13) The podcasts may also feature bonus material taped during studio rehearsal, such as additional "New Rules" that were not included in the final broadcast.

During Season 4, Maher began hosting a live chat (now called "Overtime") with his guests immediately following each broadcast. Viewers are invited to submit questions and topics for Maher and the other participants to answer and discuss. This post-show event was initially featured on HBO's website[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-14) and is currently broadcast on CNN.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher#cite_note-15)

His panel attempts to present a diverse set of views. Frequently, it consists of a liberal commentator or political figure, a conservative commentator or political figure, and a third individual who does not have as clear an ideological label, or someone with moderate beliefs. This third individual is often an actor, comedian, musician, or other entertainment figure, though many times the commentator is openly conservative or liberal.
